abstract_sentences.text: The ubiquity of closed-weight language models with public-facing APIs has generated interest in forensic methods, both for extracting hidden model details (e.g., parameters) and for identifying models by their outputs.

evidence.anchor: interest in forensic methods

abstract_sentences.text: One successful approach to these goals has been to exploit the geometric constraints imposed by the language model architecture and parameters.

evidence.anchor: geometric constraints imposed by the language model architecture

abstract_sentences.text: In this work, we show that a lesser-known geometric constraint—namely, that language model outputs lie on the surface of a high-dimensional ellipse—functions as a signature for the model and can be used to identify the source model of a given output.

evidence.anchor: outputs lie on the surface of a high-dimensional ellipse

abstract_sentences.text: This ellipse signature has unique properties that distinguish it from existing model-output association methods like language model fingerprints.

evidence.anchor: unique properties that distinguish it

abstract_sentences.text: In particular, the signature is hard to forge: without direct access to model parameters, it is practically infeasible to produce log-probabilities (logprobs) on the ellipse using currently known methods.

evidence.anchor: practically infeasible to produce log-probabilities

abstract_sentences.text: Secondly, the signature is naturally occurring, since all language models have these elliptical constraints.

evidence.anchor: naturally occurring

abstract_sentences.text: Thirdly, the signature is self-contained, in that it is detectable without access to the model inputs or the full weights.

evidence.anchor: detectable without access to the model inputs or the full weights

abstract_sentences.text: Finally, the signature is compact and redundant, as it is independently detectable in each logprob output from the model.

evidence.anchor: independently detectable in each logprob output

abstract_sentences.text: We evaluate a novel technique for extracting the ellipse from small models and discuss the practical hurdles that make it infeasible for production-scale models.

evidence.anchor: extracting the ellipse from small models

abstract_sentences.text: Finally, we use ellipse signatures to propose a protocol for language model output verification, analogous to cryptographic symmetric-key message authentication systems.

evidence.anchor: message authentication systems

final_judgment.single_storyline: Final normalization maps a hidden-state sphere through an affine/unembedding head to a model-specific high-dimensional ellipse. Centered API logprobs retain that constraint, so ellipse distance identifies the source and ellipse-fitting cost supplies practical forgery resistance.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main text keeps RMSNorm geometry, inverse-affine verification, cross-model Figure 3, smoothing/sample diagnostics, analytic sample cost, runtime extrapolation, MAC diagram, replay attack, and three explicit discussion limitations.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Centering identities, recovered reparameterization, Eq. (5)-(11) proof, layer-norm Algorithm 2, solver details, norm histograms, and logit-transformation boundaries move to Appendix A-H. The move preserves the main causal chain but makes full audit dependent on the appendix.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 2 reduces the geometry barrier, Figure 7 reduces the protocol barrier, Algorithm 1 makes extraction concrete, and Table 1 translates asymptotic growth into samples, dollars, and years.
final_judgment.largest_gap: Forgery resistance depends on the absence of a currently known fitting-free attack, while production claims rely on small-model measurements, degree-6 extrapolation, and estimated or hypothetical pricing. The protocol authenticates individual vectors, not full sequence provenance.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For a natural constraint presented as a security or verification capability, place verifiability, attacker-visible data, computational cost, unknown attacks, and replay boundaries on one evidence chain, and label measured, estimated, and hypothetical quantities.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule fits black-box ML systems with geometric or operational constraints. A paper with a cryptographic reduction or deployed verifier still needs its security game, calibration, and end-to-end deployment evidence.
